newsitem.title: UK: Europe/Med oil refineries head for negative margin.
newsitem.headline: Europe/Med oil refineries head for negative margin.

text.p: Profit margins at refineries in Europe and the Mediterranen slipped into negative territory last week as crude oil prices soared.

Friday's 80 cent rally in London's Brent crude futures and the 82 cent upturn in New York crude futures capped a dismal week for refinery operators, who now look set for further pain in the days ahead.

Simple hydroskimming plants in Europe running Brent Blend and Mediterranean units processing Urals crude were losing money on refining last week, according to Reuters calculations using standard product yields.

Brent's $2.50 a barrel rise since the start of May left northern European hydroskimming plants with an average 19 cent loss on each barrel processed last week. Average loss in the Mediterranean on the week was 16 cents a barrel.
Margins calculated at close of business on Friday were down to a loss of 25 cents in Europe and stood at a painful 66 cents per barrel in the red in the Mediterranean.
As in February and March, when margins were at similarly low levels, refiners have begun to cut throughput.
Texaco last week cut 20 percent of its output at the 400,000 barrel per day Nerefco refinery in Rotterdam of which it owns 35 percent. British Petroleum owns the other 65 percent.

Although many of the refineries in the area are complex units that are still profitable, they were also reported to be considering cutting back. Friday's surge in crude will add weight to the argument, traders said.

Gasoline and gas oil prices have climbed in Europe and the Mediterranean, but not as strongly as crude. However, fuel has failed to respond, with demand sluggish, which has put most pressure on margins, operators said.

In the U.S. gasoline prices have risen, allowing refineries there to buck the trend and increase their profitability. A U.S. plant running Brent made $1.58 a barrel last week, compared to $1.46 a week earlier.
Refinery margins were still strongest in Singapore but are now below the $3.22 a barrel average for 1996. A complex plant made $2.74 profit a barrel last week, a level not dipped too since January.
Simple, hydroskimming plants in the Far East are edging closer to unprofitability, making just 10 cents a barrel on Friday's prices.

Margins were hit by diesel prices falling at the end of a regional buying spree by one large trader, and were expected to continue under pressure into the third quarter in Asia as refineries come out of maintenance.
